context: 10. INDEMNIFICATION. Each Party (the "Indemnifying Party") shall defend, indemnify and hold harmless the other Party, its affiliates, and their respective officers, directors, employees and agents (the "Indemnified Parties") from and against any and all third-party claims, losses, damages, liabilities, judgments, settlements, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees) arising out of or relating to: (a) any breach of this Agreement by the Indemnifying Party; (b) the gross negligence or willful misconduct of the Indemnifying Party; or (c) the Indemnifying Party's violation of any applicable law. The Indemnified Party shall promptly notify the Indemnifying Party in writing of any claim and shall provide reasonable cooperation. The Indemnifying Party shall have sole control over the defense and settlement of the claim, provided that any settlement that imposes obligations on the Indemnified Party requires the Indemnified Party's prior written consent.
query: When does the indemnifying party owe indemnification under this clause?
grounded_response: Indemnification is owed when a third-party claim arises out of a breach of the Agreement, gross negligence or willful misconduct, or a violation of applicable law by the indemnifying party.
ungrounded_response: Indemnification is owed for any third-party claim regardless of cause, including ordinary negligence, and the indemnifying party must pay punitive damages.

context: 8.2 Limitation of Liability. EXCEPT FOR LIABILITY ARISING FROM (A) BREACH OF SECTION 5 (CONFIDENTIALITY), (B) THE INDEMNIFICATION OBLIGATIONS IN SECTION 10, OR (C) GROSS NEGLIGENCE OR WILLFUL MISCONDUCT, EACH PARTY'S AGGREGATE LIABILITY UNDER THIS AGREEMENT WILL NOT EXCEED THE FEES PAID OR PAYABLE BY CUSTOMER IN THE TWELVE MONTHS PRECEDING THE EVENT GIVING RISE TO LIABILITY. IN NO EVENT WILL EITHER PARTY BE LIABLE FOR INDIRECT, INCIDENTAL, CONSEQUENTIAL, SPECIAL, EXEMPLARY, OR PUNITIVE DAMAGES, INCLUDING LOST PROFITS, LOST REVENUE, OR LOST DATA, EVEN IF ADVISED OF THE POSSIBILITY.
query: What is the cap on liability and what carves it out?
grounded_response: Each party's aggregate liability is capped at the fees paid or payable by the customer in the twelve months preceding the event, with carveouts for breach of confidentiality, indemnification obligations, and gross negligence or willful misconduct.
ungrounded_response: Each party's aggregate liability is capped at the fees paid in the twenty-four months preceding the event, with no carveouts, and includes punitive damages.

context: 12. TERM AND TERMINATION. (a) Term. This Agreement begins on the Effective Date and continues for an initial term of three (3) years, automatically renewing for additional one (1) year terms unless either party gives written notice of non-renewal at least ninety (90) days before the end of the then-current term. (b) Termination for Cause. Either party may terminate this Agreement upon thirty (30) days written notice if the other party materially breaches this Agreement and fails to cure such breach within the notice period.
query: What is the renewal mechanism and the notice period to prevent renewal?
grounded_response: The Agreement automatically renews for additional one-year terms unless either party gives written notice of non-renewal at least ninety days before the end of the then-current term.
ungrounded_response: The Agreement automatically renews for additional five-year terms unless the customer gives sixty days written notice of non-renewal.

context: Section 6.4 Most Favored Customer. Vendor represents that, for the duration of this Agreement, the prices and discounts charged to Customer will be no less favorable than those charged by Vendor to any other customer of comparable size and volume. If Vendor offers more favorable terms to a comparable customer, Vendor shall promptly notify Customer and extend such terms retroactively to the date such terms were first offered to the other customer.
query: What does the most-favored-customer clause require Vendor to do if it offers better terms to a similar customer?
grounded_response: Vendor must promptly notify Customer and extend the more favorable terms retroactively to the date those terms were first offered to the other comparable customer.
ungrounded_response: Vendor must offer Customer a 10% discount on all future invoices but is not required to apply the better terms retroactively.

context: Section 14. ASSIGNMENT. Neither party may assign or transfer this Agreement, in whole or in part, without the prior written consent of the other party, which shall not be unreasonably withheld; provided, however, that either party may assign this Agreement without consent in connection with a merger, acquisition, corporate reorganization, or sale of all or substantially all of its assets, provided that the assignee assumes in writing all of the assigning party's obligations hereunder.
query: When can a party assign the agreement without the other party's consent?
grounded_response: A party may assign without consent in connection with a merger, acquisition, corporate reorganization, or sale of all or substantially all of its assets, provided the assignee assumes the assigning party's obligations in writing.
ungrounded_response: A party may assign without consent at any time as long as it provides thirty days' notice to the other party.

context: Article 33 GDPR. Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority. 1. In the case of a personal data breach, the controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority competent in accordance with Article 55, unless the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. Where the notification to the supervisory authority is not made within 72 hours, it shall be accompanied by reasons for the delay.
query: Within what timeframe must a controller notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach, and is there an exception?
grounded_response: The controller must notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of the breach, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.
ungrounded_response: The controller must notify the supervisory authority within 24 hours, with no exceptions, and must also notify all affected data subjects within the same period.

context: Article 17 GDPR. Right to erasure ('right to be forgotten'). 1. The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller the erasure of personal data concerning him or her without undue delay and the controller shall have the obligation to erase personal data without undue delay where one of the following grounds applies: (a) the personal data are no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which they were collected or otherwise processed; (b) the data subject withdraws consent on which the processing is based and where there is no other legal ground for the processing; (c) the data subject objects to the processing pursuant to Article 21(1) and there are no overriding legitimate grounds for the processing.
query: On what grounds may a data subject obtain erasure of personal data under Article 17?
grounded_response: Erasure is required where the data are no longer necessary for the original purposes, where consent is withdrawn and there is no other legal ground, or where the data subject objects to processing under Article 21(1) and no overriding legitimate grounds exist.
ungrounded_response: Erasure is required only when the data subject pays an administrative fee and provides a written request signed by a notary.

context: Article 83(5) GDPR. Infringements of the following provisions shall, in accordance with paragraph 2, be subject to administrative fines up to 20 000 000 EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 4 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher: (a) the basic principles for processing, including conditions for consent, pursuant to Articles 5, 6, 7 and 9; (b) the data subjects' rights pursuant to Articles 12 to 22; (c) the transfers of personal data to a recipient in a third country or an international organisation pursuant to Articles 44 to 49.
query: What is the maximum administrative fine under Article 83(5) GDPR?
grounded_response: Up to 20,000,000 EUR or, in the case of an undertaking, up to 4% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher.
ungrounded_response: Up to 50,000,000 EUR or 10% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is lower.

context: Article 9 EU AI Act. Risk management system. 1. A risk management system shall be established, implemented, documented and maintained in relation to high-risk AI systems. 2. The risk management system shall be understood as a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of a high-risk AI system, requiring regular systematic review and updating. It shall comprise the following steps: (a) the identification and analysis of the known and reasonably foreseeable risks that the high-risk AI system can pose to health, safety or fundamental rights; (b) the estimation and evaluation of the risks that may emerge when the high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse; (c) the evaluation of other risks possibly arising, based on the analysis of data gathered from the post-market monitoring system referred to in Article 72.
query: What kind of risks must Article 9's risk management system identify and analyse?
grounded_response: It must identify and analyse the known and reasonably foreseeable risks that the high-risk AI system can pose to health, safety, or fundamental rights, including risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse.
ungrounded_response: It must identify only the financial risks to the provider and the reputational risks to the deploying organisation.

context: Article 14 EU AI Act. Human oversight. 1. High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use. 4. Human oversight shall aim to prevent or minimise the risks to health, safety or fundamental rights that may emerge when a high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse, in particular when such risks persist despite the application of other requirements set out in this Section.
query: What is the purpose of human oversight under Article 14?
grounded_response: Human oversight aims to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights that may emerge when a high-risk AI system is used as intended or under reasonably foreseeable misuse, particularly when those risks persist despite other requirements.
ungrounded_response: Human oversight is required only to validate billing accuracy and to approve user license assignments.

context: Schrems II (C-311/18). On 16 July 2020 the Court of Justice of the European Union invalidated the EU-US Privacy Shield framework as a valid mechanism for transferring personal data to the United States, finding that US surveillance laws (in particular Section 702 FISA and Executive Order 12333) did not provide a level of data protection essentially equivalent to that guaranteed within the EU. The Court upheld the validity of Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) but emphasised that data exporters must verify, on a case-by-case basis, whether the law of the third country ensures adequate protection and may need to put in place supplementary measures.
query: What did the CJEU decide about the EU-US Privacy Shield and Standard Contractual Clauses in Schrems II?
grounded_response: The CJEU invalidated the EU-US Privacy Shield because US surveillance laws did not ensure essentially equivalent data protection, but it upheld the validity of Standard Contractual Clauses while requiring data exporters to verify adequacy case-by-case and to add supplementary measures where needed.
ungrounded_response: The CJEU upheld both the EU-US Privacy Shield and Standard Contractual Clauses without restriction and ruled that no supplementary measures are required.

context: Cambridge Analytica / Facebook FTC settlement (2019). The US Federal Trade Commission imposed a USD 5 billion civil penalty on Facebook (now Meta) for violations of a 2012 FTC consent order requiring Facebook to give users clear and prominent notice and obtain their express consent before sharing their data beyond their privacy settings. The settlement also required Facebook to implement new privacy oversight measures, including the establishment of an independent privacy committee on its board and a privacy compliance officer.
query: What was the size of the FTC penalty against Facebook in 2019 and what oversight changes were required?
grounded_response: The FTC imposed a USD 5 billion civil penalty and required Facebook to establish an independent privacy committee on its board and a privacy compliance officer.
ungrounded_response: The FTC imposed a USD 1 billion civil penalty and only required Facebook to publish a quarterly transparency report.

context: Apple v. Pepper, 587 U.S. ___ (2019). The Supreme Court held in a 5-4 decision authored by Justice Kavanaugh that consumers who purchased apps through Apple's App Store were direct purchasers from Apple for purposes of federal antitrust law and therefore had standing to sue Apple under Illinois Brick. The Court rejected Apple's argument that consumers were only indirect purchasers because app developers, not Apple, set the prices.
query: What did Apple v. Pepper decide about consumer standing under Illinois Brick?
grounded_response: The Supreme Court held 5-4 that consumers who bought apps through the App Store were direct purchasers from Apple for federal antitrust purposes and therefore had standing to sue under Illinois Brick.
ungrounded_response: The Supreme Court unanimously held that consumers were only indirect purchasers and dismissed the antitrust claim against Apple.

context: Section 4.5 of the Data Processing Addendum. Personal Data Breach. The Processor shall notify the Controller without undue delay (and in any event within 72 hours) after becoming aware of a Personal Data Breach affecting Customer Personal Data processed by the Processor, and shall provide the Controller with such information as the Controller reasonably requires to comply with its obligations under Articles 33 and 34 GDPR. The notification shall include, where possible, the nature of the breach, the categories and approximate number of data subjects concerned, and the likely consequences.
query: Within what window must the processor notify the controller of a personal data breach, and what information must the notification include?
grounded_response: The processor must notify the controller without undue delay and within 72 hours, and the notification must include where possible the nature of the breach, the categories and approximate number of data subjects concerned, and the likely consequences.
ungrounded_response: The processor must notify the controller within 30 days, and the notification need only include the breach date and a unique identifier.

context: Annex II of the DPA — Technical and Organisational Measures. (a) Access control: Role-based access at the Processor; least-privilege; SSO + MFA. (b) Encryption: TLS for inbound and outbound traffic; AES-256 for data at rest. (c) Pseudonymisation: All Personal Data is pseudonymised before being stored in the analytics database. (d) Resilience: Multi-AZ replication; automated daily backups retained for 35 days; documented disaster recovery plan. (e) Personnel: Background-checked; trained on data protection and confidentiality.
query: What encryption standards does the DPA's Annex II require for data in transit and at rest?
grounded_response: The DPA requires TLS for inbound and outbound traffic and AES-256 for data at rest.
ungrounded_response: The DPA requires TLS 1.0 for inbound traffic only and offers no specific requirement for data at rest.

context: 11. CONFIDENTIALITY. Each party (the "Receiving Party") shall protect the Confidential Information of the other party (the "Disclosing Party") with at least the same degree of care it uses to protect its own confidential information of like importance, but in no event less than reasonable care. The Receiving Party shall not use the Disclosing Party's Confidential Information except as necessary to perform under this Agreement and shall not disclose it to any third party except (a) to its employees, contractors, and advisors who have a need to know and are bound by confidentiality obligations no less protective than those herein, or (b) as required by law, provided the Receiving Party gives the Disclosing Party prompt notice and reasonable cooperation in seeking a protective order.
query: Under what circumstances may the Receiving Party disclose Confidential Information to a third party?
grounded_response: Disclosure is permitted to employees, contractors, and advisors with a need to know who are bound by no-less-protective confidentiality obligations, or as required by law with prompt notice and reasonable cooperation in seeking a protective order.
ungrounded_response: Disclosure is permitted to any third party as long as the Receiving Party provides written notice within 60 days after disclosure.

context: Section 7. PAYMENT TERMS. Customer shall pay all undisputed invoices within thirty (30) days of the invoice date. Past-due amounts shall accrue interest at the lesser of 1.5% per month or the maximum rate permitted by applicable law. If Customer disputes any portion of an invoice in good faith, Customer shall pay the undisputed portion within the original payment period and notify Vendor in writing of the disputed portion within fifteen (15) days of the invoice date.
query: What is the interest rate on past-due amounts and how must a disputed invoice be handled?
grounded_response: Past-due amounts accrue interest at the lesser of 1.5% per month or the maximum rate permitted by law, and a disputed invoice requires the customer to pay the undisputed portion within the original 30-day window and notify Vendor in writing of the disputed portion within 15 days of the invoice date.
ungrounded_response: Past-due amounts accrue interest at 5% per month, and a disputed invoice may be withheld in full until the dispute is resolved.

context: Section 16. GOVERNING LAW; DISPUTE RESOLUTION. This Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the State of New York, without regard to its conflict of laws principles. Any dispute arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall be finally resolved by binding arbitration administered by the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) under its Rules of Arbitration, by three arbitrators appointed in accordance with the said Rules. The seat of arbitration shall be London, England. The language of arbitration shall be English.
query: What law governs the agreement and how are disputes resolved?
grounded_response: The agreement is governed by the laws of the State of New York and disputes are finally resolved by binding ICC arbitration in London, in English, before a panel of three arbitrators.
ungrounded_response: The agreement is governed by the laws of England and Wales and disputes are resolved by litigation in the courts of New York.

context: Article 50 EU AI Act. Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems. 1. Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the perspective of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use. 4. Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake shall disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.
query: What disclosure does Article 50 require for AI chat interfaces and for deepfake content?
grounded_response: Providers must ensure that natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system unless that is obvious in context, and deployers of deepfake image, audio, or video content must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.
ungrounded_response: Providers must obtain explicit consent before any user can interact with an AI system, and deepfake content must be removed from any platform within 24 hours of upload.

context: Article 26 EU AI Act. Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems. 5. Deployers shall monitor the operation of the high-risk AI system on the basis of the instructions for use and where relevant, inform providers in accordance with Article 72. Where deployers have reason to consider that the use of the high-risk AI system in accordance with the instructions may result in that AI system presenting a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), they shall, without undue delay, inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority, and shall suspend the use of that system.
query: What must a deployer do if it considers that a high-risk AI system poses a risk under Article 79(1)?
grounded_response: The deployer must without undue delay inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority, and must suspend the use of the system.
ungrounded_response: The deployer may continue to use the system for thirty days while preparing a written report and is not required to notify any authority.

context: Carpenter v. United States, 585 U.S. ___ (2018). The Supreme Court held in a 5-4 decision that the government's acquisition of historical cell-site location information (CSLI) from wireless carriers is a Fourth Amendment search that generally requires a warrant supported by probable cause. The Court declined to extend the third-party doctrine to CSLI, recognising the deeply revealing nature of the data and the involuntary, automatic nature of the cellphone-tower interaction.
query: What did Carpenter v. United States hold about government access to historical cell-site location information?
grounded_response: The Supreme Court held 5-4 that government acquisition of historical cell-site location information from wireless carriers is a Fourth Amendment search that generally requires a warrant supported by probable cause, and declined to extend the third-party doctrine to such data.
ungrounded_response: The Supreme Court held that the government may obtain historical cell-site location information without a warrant under the third-party doctrine.

context: Article 17 of Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (DORA). ICT-related incident management process. 1. Financial entities shall define, establish and implement an ICT-related incident management process to detect, manage and notify ICT-related incidents. 3. Financial entities shall record all ICT-related incidents and significant cyber threats. Financial entities shall establish appropriate procedures and processes to ensure a consistent and integrated monitoring, handling and follow-up of ICT-related incidents, to ensure that the root causes are identified, documented and addressed in order to prevent the occurrence of such incidents.
query: What process must financial entities implement under Article 17 of DORA, and what records must they keep?
grounded_response: Financial entities must implement an ICT-related incident management process to detect, manage, and notify ICT-related incidents, and must record all ICT-related incidents and significant cyber threats, with procedures to ensure consistent monitoring, handling, follow-up, and root-cause identification.
ungrounded_response: Financial entities are encouraged but not required to implement an incident management process, and only incidents involving customer financial loss must be recorded.

context: 45 CFR § 164.404 — Notification to individuals. (a) Standard. (1) General rule. A covered entity shall, following the discovery of a breach of unsecured protected health information, notify each individual whose unsecured protected health information has been, or is reasonably believed by the covered entity to have been, accessed, acquired, used, or disclosed as a result of such breach. (b) Implementation specifications: Timeliness of notification. A covered entity shall provide the notification required by paragraph (a) of this section without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach.
query: Within what window must a covered entity notify individuals after discovering a breach of unsecured PHI?
grounded_response: Notification must be made without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of the breach.
ungrounded_response: Notification must be made within 7 calendar days of the breach itself, regardless of when it was discovered.

context: 45 CFR § 164.502(b)(1) — Minimum necessary. When using or disclosing protected health information or when requesting protected health information from another covered entity or business associate, a covered entity or business associate must make reasonable efforts to limit protected health information to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose of the use, disclosure, or request. (b)(2) Exceptions. Paragraph (b)(1) of this section does not apply to: (i) Disclosures to or requests by a health care provider for treatment; (ii) Uses or disclosures made to the individual; (iii) Uses or disclosures made pursuant to an authorization under § 164.508.
query: What is the minimum-necessary standard, and which uses are exempt?
grounded_response: The minimum-necessary standard requires covered entities and business associates to make reasonable efforts to limit PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose, and it does not apply to disclosures to or requests by a health care provider for treatment, uses or disclosures made to the individual, or uses or disclosures made pursuant to an authorization under § 164.508.
ungrounded_response: The minimum-necessary standard requires that all PHI be encrypted before disclosure, and there are no exceptions for treatment, individuals, or authorizations.

context: Section 9. SERVICE LEVEL AGREEMENT. Vendor shall provide the Service with monthly uptime of at least 99.9% measured at the load balancer (excluding scheduled maintenance windows announced at least seven days in advance). If actual monthly uptime falls below the SLA, Customer shall be entitled to service credits as follows: (a) below 99.9% but at least 99.5%: 10% of monthly fees; (b) below 99.5% but at least 99.0%: 25% of monthly fees; (c) below 99.0%: 50% of monthly fees. Service credits are Customer's sole and exclusive remedy for SLA failures.
query: What service credit applies if monthly uptime falls to 99.2%, and is it Customer's only remedy?
grounded_response: Uptime of 99.2% falls in the band below 99.5% but at least 99.0%, which entitles Customer to a 25% service credit on monthly fees, and service credits are Customer's sole and exclusive remedy.
ungrounded_response: Uptime of 99.2% entitles Customer to a 50% service credit on monthly fees and to terminate the Agreement immediately for cause.
